text: You are a robber on a street of houses. nums of i is the cash in house i. You cannot rob two adjacent houses on the same night — that trips the alarm. Return the most money you can rob.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the only rule is no two neighbors together. Non-adjacent houses are all fair game, and every value is non-negative? So I never lose by taking more houses, as long as they're spread out. And are there any constraints on the input size?
Right. Values are zero to four hundred, and the array has at least one house.

Got it. Let me run through an example: two, seven, nine, three, one. If I rob houses zero, two and four, I get two plus nine plus one, twelve. Robbing houses one and three gives seven plus three, ten — worse. So the answer is twelve.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be greedy — always grab the biggest house still available. That fails: on two, three, two, greedy grabs the three, both neighbors are blocked, and it ends with three, but the best is the two ends, four. This problem reminds me of a one-dimensional DP with a take-or-skip choice: at each house I make one binary choice, rob it or skip it, and I keep the best running total. It's the same skeleton as counting ways up a staircase, with a max in place of the plus.

Here's the plan. One: dp of i is the most money from the first i houses, with dp of zero equal to zero. Two: skip house i and I keep dp of i minus one; rob it and I get dp of i minus two plus its cash. Three: take the max, and the answer is dp of n. One thing worth flagging — when I rob house i, its neighbor is off-limits, so I extend from dp of i minus two, not dp of i minus one. That single index is the whole trick. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it — and the space-optimized one too.

The table version first. I pad with a sentinel, dp of zero equals zero for zero houses, so the loop is uniform — then house i is nums of i minus one, and dp of one is just the first house. The loop takes the max of rob and skip. Then the constant-space version — only the last two values matter, and it needs no base-case special-casing: prev two and prev one start at zero, and for each money I take the max of prev one, and prev two plus money. One thing worth flagging — I compute cur first, then shift, so prev one isn't overwritten before it feeds prev two.

Let's dry-run the rolling version on two, seven, nine, three, one; expected twelve. The row that matters is the last house: skipping keeps eleven, robbing gives eleven plus one, twelve — so I rob it and return twelve, from houses two, nine and one. That matches. The greedy trap: on two, three, two, DP returns four by robbing both ends, while greedy grabs the middle three. DP keeps both the skip and rob paths alive, so a locally big value never misleads it. And a single house just returns its value.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear for both. Space is linear for the table, and constant for the rolling version. Oh, one more thing — if the houses were in a circle, so the first and last are neighbors, I'd run this linear solver twice — once without the first house, once without the last — and take the max. And if I needed the actual houses robbed, I'd keep the full dp table and backtrack.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You extended from dp of i minus two when robbing, because the neighbor is forbidden. You killed greedy with a concrete counterexample. And you gave the constant-space rolling version with the correct shift order — plus the circular follow-up. Good work.
